analysis.one_liner: Eliminates all funding for the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.
analysis.headline: A bill to cut the consumer bureau's funding to zero was referred to the House Financial Services Committee in January 2025 and has taken no further action since, with only six Republican sponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill amends the 2010 law that created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and caps the money the bureau may request at $0, striking the provisions that let it draw operating funds from the Federal Reserve. The bureau is the federal agency that writes and enforces rules on mortgages, credit cards, debt collection, and credit reporting. With its funding capped at zero, the bureau could not carry out that work.
analysis.who_benefits: If the bill passed, banks, payday and other high-cost lenders, debt collectors, and credit reporting companies would no longer face a dedicated federal regulator supervising their consumer-facing practices or bringing enforcement cases against them. Any business fined by or under investigation by the bureau would see that pressure disappear.

how_it_helps.text: The bill caps the funding the bureau's Director may request at "not more than $0." [S2] [S3]

It strikes the paragraphs of the 2010 funding provision that authorize the bureau to draw its operating money from the Federal Reserve, removing the mechanism that has funded it outside the yearly appropriations process. [S3]
For financial firms, the practical effect of a zero budget is that the bureau could not examine companies, write rules, or bring enforcement actions. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary consumers would bear the cost: no federal agency would be actively supervising mortgage servicing, credit card fees, debt collection, and credit reporting errors on their behalf, and consumers would lose the bureau as a place to take complaints and win refunds.

drawbacks.text: A $0 cap means the bureau cannot function at all; it is not a trim but a shutdown of the agency's consumer-protection work. [S2] [S3]

Because the bureau's funding comes through the Federal Reserve rather than annual appropriations, its supporters argue it is insulated from congressional pressure; this bill ends that insulation by zeroing out the funding. [S3]

An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that consumers who lose money to improper fees, faulty credit reports, or abusive debt collection would have no dedicated federal enforcer to recover it for them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit runs to financial firms that would be free of the bureau's supervision and enforcement; the cost falls on the households the bureau serves when it polices mortgages, credit cards, and debt collection. There is no offsetting consumer benefit in the bill text.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which has taken no action on it since, so nothing has happened yet.

narrative.text: Representative Keith Self introduced the bill with five original cosponsors on January 28, 2025. [S3]
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services. [S1] [S5]
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the action history. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nothing has changed: because the bill has not advanced, the bureau remains funded and consumers keep its enforcement and complaint services, while the firms the bill would relieve have not gotten that relief.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers, for now — the bill stalled

for.name: Rep. Keith Self
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap CFPB funding at $0.

for.name: 5 of 223 House Republicans
for.role: Original cosponsors (Reps. Weber of Texas, Donalds, Grothman, Tiffany, Pfluger)

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all five cosponsors are Republicans, and no Democrat is listed in support; no vote has occurred to show how the full chambers would split. [S4]

industries.note: These firms are the bureau's main subjects for supervision and enforcement on mortgages, credit cards, and fees. A zero budget removes the agency that polices their consumer practices, a gain that comes directly at consumers' expense. [S2] [S3]
The bureau has been the primary federal regulator of short-term, high-cost lending. Defunding it would leave these lenders without a dedicated federal watchdog. [S2] [S3]

industries.industry: Debt collectors and credit reporting companies
industries.note: These industries face the bureau's rules on collections practices and credit-report accuracy. Without an enforcer, complaints about wrongful collections and credit errors would go largely unanswered. [S2] [S3]

analysis.trajectory: With only six sponsors, no Democratic support, and no committee action in the months since referral, the bill is very likely to remain in committee unless House leadership or the Financial Services Committee chooses to schedule a markup, which standalone agency-defunding bills rarely receive.
